problems.stem: A syllabus clause reads 'Use of AI tools is prohibited. Violations are academic dishonesty.' Which revision best protects student design judgment?
options: Keep the ban but add 'no exceptions.'
Permit bounded use (brainstorm, self-critique, alternatives), forbid submitting generated work as one's own, and require a one-line disclosure.
Allow any AI use with no disclosure.
Ban AI only during the final week of the course.
problems.explanation: Bounded permission with disclosure keeps the learner's judgment visible instead of driving concealment.

problems.stem: Which disclosure line follows the policy's required format most completely?
options: Used Claude to generate three signaling alternatives for Frame 2; accepted one, rejected two because they added redundant on-screen text.
I confirm I did not cheat.
problems.explanation: A complete disclosure names the tool, the prompt intent, and what was accepted or rejected.

problems.stem: A student uses a screen reader's AI alt-text generator to access course images. Under a well-written policy, this should be:
options: A violation, because any AI use is banned.
Permitted assistive use, because the policy distinguishes accessibility tools from generating design work.
Permitted only if the student hides it.
Decided case by case with no written rule.
problems.explanation: A policy that names what it protects (the learner's design judgment) does not sweep assistive AI into the prohibition.

problems.stem: The instructor wants evidence the revised policy worked. Which result is the strongest signal?
options: Fewer students mentioned AI at all.
Disclosures appeared on 11 of 12 AI-assisted drafts, so the boundary of student judgment was visible and assessable.
No student asked any questions about the policy.
problems.explanation: Visible disclosures show the policy produced transparency rather than concealment.
